claim: Lymphocytes infiltrate the brain in small numbers after stroke.
source: Although lymphocytes infiltrate the brain in small number, they have been consistently demonstrated to be the most potent leukocyte subpopulation contributing to secondary inflammatory brain injury.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of post-stroke neuroinflammation

claim: Lymphocytes are the most potent leukocyte subpopulation contributing to secondary inflammatory brain injury after stroke.
source: Although lymphocytes infiltrate the brain in small number, they have been consistently demonstrated to be the most potent leukocyte subpopulation contributing to secondary inflammatory brain injury.
evidence: Referenced as consistently demonstrated in prior research

claim: TH1 cells induce type I IFN signaling in microglia after stroke.
source: Here, using a mouse model for ischemic stroke, we demonstrated that early activation of microglia in response to stroke is differentially regulated by distinct T cell subpopulations – with TH1 cells inducing a type I INF signaling in microglia and regulatory T cells (TREG) cells promoting microglial genes associated with chemotaxis.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the current study using mouse models

claim: Regulatory T cells (TREG) promote microglial genes associated with chemotaxis after stroke.
source: Here, using a mouse model for ischemic stroke, we demonstrated that early activation of microglia in response to stroke is differentially regulated by distinct T cell subpopulations – with TH1 cells inducing a type I INF signaling in microglia and regulatory T cells (TREG) cells promoting microglial genes associated with chemotaxis.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the current study using mouse models

claim: Acute treatment with engineered T cells overexpressing IL-10 administered into the cisterna magna after stroke induces a switch of microglial gene expression to a profile associated with pro-regenerative functions.
source: Acute treatment with engineered T cells overexpressing IL-10 administered into the cisterna magna after stroke induces a switch of microglial gene expression to a profile associated with pro-regenerative functions.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the current study

claim: Microglia polarization by T cell subsets did not affect the acute development of infarct volume.
source: Whereas microglia polarization by T cell subsets did not affect the acute development of the infarct volume, these findings substantiate the role of T cells in stroke by polarizing the microglial phenotype.
evidence: Observed in the experimental results of the current study

claim: T cells have been consistently identified as the invading leukocyte subpopulation with the largest impact on secondary neurodegeneration and modulation of ischemic brain damage.
source: Among peripheral leukocytes invading the injured brain, T cells have been consistently identified as the invading leukocyte subpopulation with the largest impact on secondary neurodegeneration and modulation of the ischemic brain damage (Kleinschnitz et al., 2010; Liesz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Pro-inflammatory TH1, TH17 subsets of T helper cells, and IL-17-producing γδ T cells induce secondary neurotoxicity leading to infarct expansion with worse functional outcome.
source: In particular, the pro-inflammatory TH1, TH17 subsets of THELPER cells, and IL-17-producing γδ T cells have been shown to induce secondary neurotoxicity, leading to infarct expansion with worse functional outcome (Gelderblom et al., 2012; Shichita et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Regulatory T cells (TREG) exert anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective function suppressing an excessive inflammatory reaction to the brain infarct.
source: whereas regulatory T cells (TREG) exert anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective function suppressing an excessive inflammatory reaction to the brain infarct.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: T cell accumulation is observed in the choroid plexus and meninges after stroke.
source: Recruitment of peripheral immune cells is not limited to the brain parenchyma since an accumulation of T cells is observed in the choroid plexus and the meninges after stroke (Benakis et al., 2016; Llovera et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Blocking the recruitment of peripheral effector T cells diminished neuronal damage in different cerebral ischemic models, resulting in improvement of stroke outcome.
source: Attempt in blocking the recruitment of peripheral effector T cells diminished neuronal damage in different cerebral ischemic models, resulting in improvement of stroke outcome and suggesting a possible therapeutic target (Liesz et al., 2011; Llovera et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Only a few thousand lymphocytes invade the brain after stroke compared to more than 50 times higher cell count of innate immune cells in the post-stroke brain.
source: Considering the relatively low number of only a few thousand lymphocytes invading the brain after stroke compared to more than 50 times higher cell count of innate immune cells (invading and resident) in the post-stroke brain (Gelderblom et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Microglia interact with T cells via cell-to-cell contact, cytokine-mediated communication, or antigen presentation.
source: Indeed, microglia interact with T cells via either cell-to-cell contact, cytokine-mediated communication, or antigen presentation, leading to activation/polarization of adaptive immune cells entering the brain (Goldmann and Prinz, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: T cell-microglia interaction influences the neuroinflammatory response in experimental models of multiple sclerosis.
source: T cell-microglia interaction can further influence the neuroinflammatory response in experimental models of multiple sclerosis (Dong and Yong, 2019) and possibly in stroke (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Recent evidence suggests a crosstalk between microglia and T cells as a key determinant of neuronal plasticity during recovery from brain injury.
source: In fact, recent evidence suggests a crosstalk between microglia and T cells as a key determinant of neuronal plasticity during recovery from brain injury (Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Microglia of Rag1−/− mice displayed extended ramifications and lower sphericity compared to microglia of wild-type mice at the perilesional cortex after stroke.
source: Using an automated morphological analysis of IBA1 positive cells (Heindl et al., 2018) located at the perilesional (ipsilateral) cortex, where CD3+ T cells accumulated (Figure 1B), we identified that microglia of Rag1−/− mice displayed extended ramifications and a lower sphericity compared to microglia of wild-type (WT) mice, indicating a less reactive phenotype of microglia in the absence of lymphocytes (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated through morphological analysis in the current study, shown in Figure 1C, D

claim: Microglia in Rag1−/− mice show a less reactive phenotype in the absence of lymphocytes.
source: we identified that microglia of Rag1−/− mice displayed extended ramifications and a lower sphericity compared to microglia of wild-type (WT) mice, indicating a less reactive phenotype of microglia in the absence of lymphocytes (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Inferred from morphological features observed in the current study

claim: Microglial morphology remained relatively unchanged between Rag1−/− and WT mice in the contralateral hemisphere.
source: In contrast, microglial morphology remained relatively unchanged between Rag1−/− and WT mice in the contralateral (unaffected) hemisphere which does not show recruitment of lymphocyte in considerable amounts, supporting the role of local lymphocyte infiltration for changing microglial morphology.
evidence: Observed in morphological analysis in the current study

claim: Depletion of microglia in Rag1−/− mice resulted in a significant increase of infarct volume compared to vehicle-treated Rag1−/− mice.
source: Surprisingly, we found a significant increase of the infarct volume in Rag1−/− mice depleted of microglia in comparison to vehicle-treated Rag1−/− mice, whereas depletion of microglia in WT mice has no significant effect (Figure 1G)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally using PLX5622 treatment, shown in Figure 1G

claim: Depletion of microglia in WT mice has no significant effect on infarct volume.
source: we found a significant increase of the infarct volume in Rag1−/− mice depleted of microglia in comparison to vehicle-treated Rag1−/− mice, whereas depletion of microglia in WT mice has no significant effect (Figure 1G)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally using PLX5622 treatment, shown in Figure 1G

claim: Microglia-T cell interaction is required to influence the development of the infarct.
source: These data suggest that microglia-T cell interaction is required to influence the development of the infarct.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of microglia depletion in WT vs Rag1−/− mice

claim: CD3+ T cells were localized at the infarct border 5 days after stroke.
source: CD3+ T cells were localized at the infarct border as quantified on immunohistochemistry coronal sections and represented in the cumulative topographic maps 5 days after stroke (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in the current study, shown in Figure 1C

claim: Stroke is the primary driver of transcriptomic changes in microglia at 5 days post-stroke.
source: The cell distribution across condition highlighted that stroke is the main driver of the microglial transcriptomic changes, both in WT and Rag1−/− mice (Figure 2C, right plot).
evidence: Demonstrated by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis, shown in Figure 2C

claim: Apoe and Cd74 were down-regulated in naïve Rag1−/− mice compared to naïve WT mice.
source: Volcano plots of the differentially expressed genes revealed that Apoe and Cd74 were down-regulated in naïve Rag1−/− mice, indicating that the transcriptional profile of microglia is affected by the absence of lymphocytes in homeostatic condition (Figure 2D, left plot).
evidence: Demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 2D

claim: The transcriptional profile of microglia is affected by the absence of lymphocytes in homeostatic condition.
source: Volcano plots of the differentially expressed genes revealed that Apoe and Cd74 were down-regulated in naïve Rag1−/− mice, indicating that the transcriptional profile of microglia is affected by the absence of lymphocytes in homeostatic condition (Figure 2D, left plot).
evidence: Inferred from differential gene expression in naïve Rag1−/− vs WT mice

claim: Several disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes were up-regulated in Rag1−/− mice after stroke, including Apoe, Cd74, Cstb, Lgals3, and Lyz2.
source: Interestingly, several genes, known to define the signature of the disease-associated microglia (DAMs, Keren-Shaul et al., 2017), were up-regulated in Rag1−/− mice after stroke (Apoe, Cd74, Cstb, Lgals3, and Lyz2; Figure 2D, right plot).
evidence: Demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis with reference to known DAM markers, shown in Figure 2D

claim: 67 stroke-associated microglial genes were common to both WT and Rag1−/− mice, including the majority of the DAM signature.
source: When we compared the stroke-associated microglial genes between WT and Rag1−/− mice, we found that 67 genes – including the majority of the DAM signature (Apoe, B2m, Cstb, Lgals3, Lyz2, and Spp1) – were not specific to the lymphocyte deficiency (Figure 2E)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 2E

claim: 120 stroke-associated microglial genes were only present in Rag1−/− mice, including genes involved in cytokine signaling and chemotaxis.
source: whereas 120 stroke-associated microglial genes were only present in mice lacking lymphocytes, such as genes involved in cytokine signaling and chemotaxis (i.e. Cd74, Ccl2, Ccl7, H2-Ab1, Infgr1, Mif, Pf4, and Tnf).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative gene expression analysis

claim: Lymphocytes influence the transition of a microglia subpopulation from the homeostatic to the reactive state.
source: Interestingly, the number of microglial cells in stroke Rag1−/− increased in the end cluster and was decreased along the trajectory path 2 in comparison to stroke WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that lymphocytes influence the transition of a microglia subpopulation from the homoeostatic to the reactive state.
evidence: Inferred from trajectory analysis showing differential cell distribution, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Genes associated with ribosomal metabolic processes and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins were specifically enriched in microglia of Rag1−/− mice along the trajectory from homeostatic to reactive state.
source: Differential gene expression analysis between the root and end clusters of the trajectory path 2 in WT and Rag1−/− mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) revealed that genes associated with ribosomal metabolic processes and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins were specifically enriched, whereas genes associated with phagocytosis were down-regulated in microglia of Rag1−/− mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis along trajectory, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D

claim: Genes associated with phagocytosis were down-regulated in microglia of Rag1−/− mice along the trajectory from homeostatic to reactive state.
source: Differential gene expression analysis between the root and end clusters of the trajectory path 2 in WT and Rag1−/− mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) revealed that genes associated with ribosomal metabolic processes and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins were specifically enriched, whereas genes associated with phagocytosis were down-regulated in microglia of Rag1−/− mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis along trajectory, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D

claim: The absence of lymphocytes significantly reduces microglial genes associated with macrophage activation state.
source: Gene sets which were significantly different between WT and Rag1−/− mice after stroke revealed that the absence of lymphocytes significantly reduces microglial genes associated with macrophage activation state (G6: Foxp1, Syk Shi et al., 2008; Tabata et al., 2020)
evidence: Demonstrated by gene set analysis with citations to support gene function

claim: Genes associated with cytokine/chemokine stimulus were enriched in Rag1−/− microglia compared to WT microglia after stroke.
source: whereas genes associated with cytokine/chemokine stimulus were enriched (G3: Il1b, Tnf, Csf1, and Ccl2) in Rag1−/− in comparison to WT microglia (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene set analysis, shown in Figure 2F

claim: T cells are 14 times more abundant than B cells in the ipsilesional hemisphere 5 days after stroke in WT mice.
source: First, we demonstrate that T cells are 14 times more abundant than B cells in the ipsilesional hemisphere in WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A

claim: The abundance of myeloid cell subsets is not affected by Rag1 gene deletion.
source: In addition, the abundance of myeloid cell subsets is not affected by the Rag1 gene deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B

claim: The transcriptional profile of microglia induced by TREG cells was more similar to vehicle treated Rag1−/− mice than microglial gene expression induced by TH1.
source: The transcriptional profile of microglia induced by TREG cells was more similar to vehicle treated Rag1−/− mice (named control [CT]) than microglial gene expression induced by TH1, as shown in the heatmap and volcano plots of the differentially expressed genes (p<0.05 and |fold change|>1.5) with 34 and 12 microglial genes regulated in TH1 or TREG conditions compared to control injection, respectively (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 3B, C

claim: TH1 cells regulate 34 microglial genes compared to control injection.
source: The transcriptional profile of microglia induced by TREG cells was more similar to vehicle treated Rag1−/− mice (named control [CT]) than microglial gene expression induced by TH1, as shown in the heatmap and volcano plots of the differentially expressed genes (p<0.05 and |fold change|>1.5) with 34 and 12 microglial genes regulated in TH1 or TREG conditions compared to control injection, respectively (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 3B, C

claim: TREG cells regulate 12 microglial genes compared to control injection.
source: The transcriptional profile of microglia induced by TREG cells was more similar to vehicle treated Rag1−/− mice (named control [CT]) than microglial gene expression induced by TH1, as shown in the heatmap and volcano plots of the differentially expressed genes (p<0.05 and |fold change|>1.5) with 34 and 12 microglial genes regulated in TH1 or TREG conditions compared to control injection, respectively (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 3B, C

claim: TH1-dependent microglial pathways are associated with antigen presentation, response to cytokines, and regulation of type I IFN.
source: Gene ontology analysis of the differentially up-regulated genes revealed TH1-dependent pathways associated with antigen presentation, response to cytokines, and regulation of type I INF, whereas TREG-dependent microglial genes were associated with chemotaxis (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 3D

claim: TREG-dependent microglial genes are associated with chemotaxis.
source: Gene ontology analysis of the differentially up-regulated genes revealed TH1-dependent pathways associated with antigen presentation, response to cytokines, and regulation of type I INF, whereas TREG-dependent microglial genes were associated with chemotaxis (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 3D

claim: TH1 polarized microglia toward an antigen-immunocompetent phenotype with expression of Cd74 and Lag3.
source: In particular, we found that TH1 polarized microglia toward an antigen-immunocompetent phenotype (Cd74 and Lag3) and expression of INF response-related genes (Irf7 and Stat1).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis in the current study

claim: TH1 polarized microglia express IFN response-related genes including Irf7 and Stat1.
source: In particular, we found that TH1 polarized microglia toward an antigen-immunocompetent phenotype (Cd74 and Lag3) and expression of INF response-related genes (Irf7 and Stat1).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis in the current study

claim: The microglial response profile induced by TH1 was previously associated with a pronounced immune response during the later stages of neurodegeneration.
source: This profile of microglial response was previously associated with a pronounced immune response during the later stages of neurodegeneration (Mathys et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: TH1-mediated effects on the microglial transcriptomic profile were associated with an increase of Trem2 expression compared to microglia primed by TREG cells.
source: In addition, after experimental stroke, the TH1-mediated effects on the microglial transcriptomic profile were associated with an increase of Trem2 expression, a key marker of DAM in various brain disorders, in comparison to microglia primed by TREG cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by smFISH analysis, shown in Figure 3E

claim: TREG cells promoted the expression of chemokines/cytokines in microglia including Ccl2, Ccl7, and Cxcl10.
source: In contrast, TREG cells promoted the expression of chemokines/cytokines in microglia (Ccl2, Ccl7, and Cxcl10), which can have either pro-regenerative or detrimental effects such as the regulation of leukocyte chemotaxis to the injured brain (Llovera et al., 2017), mechanisms of protective preconditioning (Garcia-Bonilla et al., 2014) or promoting neuronal stem cell recruitment and angiogenesis (Andres et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis with citations to support potential functions

claim: Microglia displayed a reactive state with more spherical and less branched morphology in TH1 cell-injected compared to TREG-injected mice.
source: Microglia displayed a reactive state as shown by a more spherical and less branched morphology in TH1 cell-injected compared to TREG-injected mice (Figure 3F) similarly to microglia in Rag1−/− mice (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis, shown in Figure 3F

claim: Morphological changes in microglia induced by differentiated T helper cells were observed in both ipsilesional and contralateral hemispheres.
source: Interestingly, these morphological changes were not only restricted to the ipsilesional hemisphere as seen in Rag1−/− not reconstituted with T cell subsets (Figure 1D) but were also observed in the contralateral hemisphere, suggesting possible brain-wide effects of differentiated THELPER cells injected to the CSF compartment.
evidence: Observed in morphological analysis with inference about brain-wide effects

claim: Intra-CM injection of eGFP-labeled TH1 cells to Rag1−/− mice after stroke was primarily recruited to the ischemic brain parenchyma but was additionally localized in border tissues including the meninges.
source: In accordance, we found that intra-CM injection of eGFP-labeled TH1 cells to Rag1–/– mice after stroke was primarily recruited to the ischemic brain parenchyma but was additionally localized in border tissues including the meninges, and some CM-injected cells even circulated and could be detected in the spleen ( Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence, shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Some CM-injected TH1 cells circulated and could be detected in the spleen.
source: In accordance, we found that intra-CM injection of eGFP-labeled TH1 cells to Rag1–/– mice after stroke was primarily recruited to the ischemic brain parenchyma but was additionally localized in border tissues including the meninges, and some CM-injected cells even circulated and could be detected in the spleen ( Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry, shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: No difference in infarct volumes was observed between WT and Rag1−/− mice.
source: Importantly, no difference in infarct volumes was observed between WT and Rag1−/– mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Demonstrated by infarct volumetry, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: No difference in infarct volumes was observed in TH1 or TREG-supplemented Rag1−/− mice.
source: Importantly, no difference in infarct volumes was observed between WT and Rag1−/– mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and in TH1 or TREG-supplemented Rag1–/– mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated by infarct volumetry, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: eTc-IL10 treatment did not affect infarct volumes after stroke.
source: We investigated whether eTc-IL10 treatment affected stroke outcome but did not find any difference in infarct volumes between conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by infarct volumetry, shown in Figure 4D

claim: Mice receiving eTc-IL10 injection in the CM had a significant improvement of functional outcome at 48 hr after stroke as shown by reduced forelimb asymmetry.
source: In contrast, mice receiving eTc-IL10 injection in the CM had a significant improvement of functional outcome at 48 hr after stroke as shown by a reduced forelimb asymmetry in comparison to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by cylinder test behavioral assessment, shown in Figure 4E

claim: Several genes associated with a DAM profile were down-regulated in mice treated with eTc-IL10, including Cd68, Apoe, Trem2, Tyrobp, and Cst7.
source: Interestingly, we found that several genes associated with a DAM profile were down-regulated in mice treated with eTc-IL10 such as Cd68, Apoe, Trem2, Tyrobp, and Cst7 (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: T cell-derived IL-10 overexpression increased pathways associated with chemokine responses.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed that T cell-derived IL-10 overexpression increased pathways associated with chemokine responses – similarly to Rag1−/− mice reconstituted with TREG cells – and the down-regulation of several microglial effector functions such as spine pruning, phagocytosis, and complement activation (Figure 4G).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 4G

claim: T cell-derived IL-10 overexpression resulted in down-regulation of microglial effector functions including spine pruning, phagocytosis, and complement activation.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed that T cell-derived IL-10 overexpression increased pathways associated with chemokine responses – similarly to Rag1−/− mice reconstituted with TREG cells – and the down-regulation of several microglial effector functions such as spine pruning, phagocytosis, and complement activation (Figure 4G).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 4G

claim: eTc-IL10 treatment resulted in a reduction of Trem2 mRNA in Cx3cr1+ microglia.
source: This anti-inflammatory effect of eTc-IL10 treatment on microglia was confirmed by a reduction of Trem2 mRNA in Cx3cr1+microglia from eTc-IL10 compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: Demonstrated by smFISH analysis, shown in Figure 4H

claim: Acute intra-CM administration of eTc-IL10 induces a switch of the microglia gene signature possibly involved in promoting post-stroke recovery mechanisms.
source: Since we observed a down regulation of genes associated with synapse pruning (C1qa, C1qb, and C1qc), microglia activation, and phagocytosis (Apoe, Ctss, Trem2, and Cd68) in mice treated with eTc-IL10, we postulate that acute intra-CM administration of eTc-IL10 induces a switch of the microglia gene signature possibly involved in promoting post-stroke recovery mechanisms.
evidence: Speculated based on observed gene expression changes

claim: The microglia-polarizing effect of different T helper cell subpopulations is mainly mediated via their specific cytokine/chemokine secretion pattern.
source: Our results from transcriptomic analysis suggest that the microglia-polarizing effect of different THELPER cell subpopulations is mainly mediated via their specific cytokine/chemokine secretion pattern.
evidence: Inferred from transcriptomic analysis results

claim: Microglia that were challenged with TH1 cells expressed an up-regulation of genes associated with type I IFN signaling.
source: Microglia that were challenged with TH1 cells expressed an up-regulation of genes associated with type I INF signaling – the key cytokine secreted by the TH1 subpopulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis in the current study

claim: TREG cells modulated a gene set in microglia associated with chemotaxis-mediated mechanisms including Ccl2, Ccl7, and Cxcl10.
source: In contrast, TREG cells modulated a gene set in microglia associated with chemotaxis-mediated mechanisms (Ccl2, Ccl7, and Cxcl10).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis in the current study

claim: TREG cells mediate a down-regulation of Trem2, a marker associated with reactive microglia.
source: We also observed that TREG cells mediate a down-regulation of markers associated with reactive microglia such as the expression of Trem2, which have previously been described to be regulated by the TREG-cytokine IL-10 (Shemer et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated in the current study with support from cited prior research

claim: IL-10 has a direct role in modulating microglial function.
source: These previous and our own results here clearly show the direct role of IL-10 in modulating microglial function.
evidence: Inferred from current and prior research results

claim: Adult human microglial cells co-cultured with T lymphocytes show an enrichment of IL-10 secretion upon direct cell-cell contact.
source: Likewise, using adult human microglial cells co-culture with T lymphocytes, others demonstrated an enrichment of IL-10 secretion upon direct cell-cell contact (Chabot et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of IL-10 is sufficient to modulate the neuroinflammatory response after experimental stroke.
source: In addition, we previously reported using whole genome sequencing that intracerebroventricular injection of IL-10 is sufficient to modulate the neuroinflammatory response after experimental stroke (Liesz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: IL-10 has a short half-life of less than 1 hour and limited bioactivity after in vivo administration as a recombinant protein.
source: An important caveat and potential key reason for the so far still pending success in harnessing the therapeutic function of IL-10 are its short half-life (less than 1 hr) and limited bioactivity after in vivo administration as a recombinant protein (Le et al., 1997; Saxena et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Systemic IL-10 application can have considerable and unforeseen side-effects due to the potentially divergent function of IL-10 on inflamed and homeostatic tissue.
source: Moreover, the systemic IL-10 application can have considerable and unforeseen side-effects due to the potentially divergent function of IL-10 on inflamed and homeostatic tissue, including direct effects on neurons, astrocytes, endothelial cells, and other cellular constituents of physiological brain function (Saraiva et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: IL-10 overexpression in T cells modulated microglial genes involved in the complement pathway, phagocytosis, and synaptic pruning and was associated with better functional outcome after stroke.
source: An important finding in this study was the observation that IL-10 overexpression in T cells modulated microglial genes involved in the complement pathway, phagocytosis, and synaptic pruning and was associated with a better functional outcome after stroke.
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis and behavioral testing in the current study

claim: Complement factors are localized to developing CNS synapses during periods of active synapse elimination and are required for normal brain wiring.
source: Complement factors are localized to developing CNS synapses during periods of active synapse elimination and are required for normal brain wiring (Schafer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Inactive synapses tagged with complement proteins such as C1q may be eliminated by microglial cells.
source: Inactive synapses tagged with complement proteins such as C1q may be eliminated by microglial cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Early synapse loss is a hallmark of several neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Likewise in the mature brain, early synapse loss is a hallmark of several neurodegenerative diseases (Stephan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Complement proteins are profoundly up-regulated in many CNS diseases prior to signs of neuron loss.
source: Indeed, complement proteins are profoundly up-regulated in many CNS diseases prior to signs of neuron loss, suggesting mechanisms of complement-mediated synapse elimination regulated by microglia potentially driving disease progression (Stephan et al., 2012) and stroke recovery.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: T cells overexpressing IL-10 down-regulate the complement system in microglia and prevent excessive elimination of synapses.
source: It is therefore conceivable that T cells overexpressing IL-10 down-regulate the complement system in microglia and prevent excessive elimination of synapse and consequently protect against neuronal dysfunction.
evidence: Speculated based on observed gene expression changes and known mechanisms

claim: Microglia effector function has been shown to be neuroprotective by tightly monitoring neuronal status through somatic junctions.
source: This is particularly of interest because microglia effector function has not only been associated with inflammatory neurodegenerative processes but recently also been shown to be neuroprotective (Szalay et al., 2016) by tightly monitoring neuronal status through somatic junctions (Cserép et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Microglia interact with the extra-neuronal space by regulating the elimination of existing synapses and by modifying the extracellular matrix to enable efficient synaptic remodeling.
source: Microglia interact with the extra-neuronal space by not only regulating the elimination of existing synapses but also by modifying the extracellular matrix to enable efficient synaptic remodeling (Zaki and Cai, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: T cell-dependent regulation of microglial genes includes genes that can mediate extracellular matrix modifications involved in phagocytosis and proteases.
source: Accordingly, we found T cell-dependent regulation of several microglial genes that can mediate such extracellular matrix modifications involved in phagocytosis and proteases (Clstn1 and Mmp12, cathepsins and MMPs, respectively).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression analysis in the current study

claim: At the acute time point studied, the transcriptomic changes in microglia are mainly attributed to their reactivity to the tissue injury itself.
source: Whereas at this acute time point, the transcriptomic changes in microglia are mainly attributed to their reactivity to the tissue injury itself, we have been able to demonstrate that brain-invading T cells can specifically 'fine-tune' the transition of the stroke-associated microglia to a distinct cell morphology and transcriptomic profile.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing stroke as the main driver of changes

claim: Brain-invading T cells can specifically fine-tune the transition of stroke-associated microglia to a distinct cell morphology and transcriptomic profile.
source: Whereas at this acute time point, the transcriptomic changes in microglia are mainly attributed to their reactivity to the tissue injury itself, we have been able to demonstrate that brain-invading T cells can specifically 'fine-tune' the transition of the stroke-associated microglia to a distinct cell morphology and transcriptomic profile.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological and transcriptomic analysis in the current study

claim: Anti-inflammatory TREG cells induce a shift of microglial genes associated with a homeostatic state and immune cell recruitment.
source: Our data suggested that the anti-inflammatory TREG cells induce a shift of microglial genes associated with a homeostatic state and immune cell recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from gene expression analysis results in the current study

claim: The development of engineered T cells could have important translational implication by targeting a specific effector function of microglia with a relevant impact on the chronic progression of stroke pathobiology.
source: We postulate that the development of engineered T cells could have important translational implication by targeting a specific effector function of microglia with a relevant impact on the chronic progression of stroke pathobiology.
evidence: Speculated based on the experimental findings

claim: Maximal cerebral leukocyte infiltration occurs at the lesion border 5 days after stroke.
source: Microglia were analyzed 5 days after stroke at the lesion border because this region and this acute time point were identified as the maximal cerebral leukocyte infiltration as previously published (Llovera et al., 2017) and exemplified in (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and exemplified in Figure 1B

claim: PLX5622 incorporated in mouse diet for 2 weeks prior to stroke almost completely depleted microglia from the brain.
source: Images show that 2 weeks of PLX5622-diet almost completely depleted microglia from the brain (IBA1, red; 4',6-Diamidin-2-phenylindol [DAPI], blue), scale bar: 500 µm.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry, shown in Figure 1F

claim: Five clusters of CD45+CD11b+ cells were annotated as microglial cells based on expression of homeostatic and reactive microglia markers.
source: Based on the expression of previously defined markers of homeostatic and reactive microglia per cell cluster (high gene expression of Fcrls, P2ry12, and Trem2; low expression of Itgax, Ccr2, and Lyz2; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Miron and Priller, 2020; Prinz and Priller, 2014), five clusters were annotated as microglial cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Determined by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis using previously defined markers, shown in Figure 2B

claim: Microglial subpopulations show transcriptomic profiles preferentially associated with either homeostatic microglial function (clusters 0, 1, 4, and 6) or reactive microglia (clusters 2, 3, 5, and 7).
source: We then performed a subclustering analysis on only the microglia cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and identified subpopulations showing either a transcriptomic profile preferentially associated with homeostatic microglial function (clusters 0, 1, 4, and 6) or a profile of reactive microglia (clusters 2, 3, 5, and 7; Figure 2C, left plot and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by subclustering analysis, shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: PAGA revealed two distinct paths with high connectivity from the homeostatic microglia cluster to the reactive microglia cluster.
source: Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) revealed two distinct paths with high connectivity from the homeostatic (naïve) microglia cluster (root cluster) to the reactive (stroke) microglia cluster (end cluster; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by trajectory inference analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: eTc-IL10 cells were located in the meningeal compartment and could contribute to functional recovery by resolving inflammation at border structures or providing IL-10 to the brain parenchyma along CSF flow.
source: Interestingly, eTc-IL10 cells did not exclusively invade the injured brain but were also located in the meningeal compartment and could additionally contribute to functional recovery by resolving inflammation at these border structures or providing IL-10 to the brain parenchyma along CSF flow.
evidence: Speculated based on observed cell localization

claim: Meningeal immune cell accumulation occurs after stroke.
source: This concept is in accordance with previous observations of meningeal immune cell accumulation after stroke (Benakis et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Meningeal T cell-derived cytokines may enter the brain via CSF flow and paravascular spaces.
source: and that meningeal T cell-derived cytokines may enter the brain via CSF flow and paravascular spaces (Iliff et al., 2012).
